title: Slide lubricant and caring for the instrument
summary: Using kitty-kill sale and kerosene on the slide, mopping out the horn, and washing it.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns

blocks.x: Did they always use oil in the old days for sliding? The trumpet players have to spit on the valve, you know?

Yeah, well, I used to use, I used oil too, but oil, it kept us buying so expensive in a way. You had to be buying but 25 cents a bottle, but you would use it, yeah, see. What I did, I used kitty-kill sale. Kitty-kill sale. Just take the kitty-kill sale and throw it on your slide all the way down, grease your slides good, and after you grease your slides with this kitty-kill sale, you put a little kerosene on it, and that slide will fly. And it doesn't evaporate as fast? No, it doesn't evaporate as fast. But they haven't used Vaseline, or is that too stiff? It is too stiff. A lot of fellas used it, but it's hard dragging. I tried it once, but I couldn't, couldn't get away at all. See, it's just stiff, hold your hand. Anything else about the care of instruments? Well, the care of instruments should be always, it should be mopped out after any engagement that you play. You should take that instrument and mop it out. You'd have one of those long rods and run it through there. Go through the slides and everything? Yeah, through the slides and through the other part. See, that is, you wouldn't go, you have to take it off. you had a long rod with a little bit of flesh rag on it or some kind of a, you might say, a woolen cloth on the end. And you carry it through the slides on the outside and sometimes you push out dirt, like dirt. You know, that's when your slide working, it throws that grease down and it goes in there. You push that out. Well,
I used to see, Buck Johnson and I used to record him, sometimes he would run water through his trombone under a faucet.
Yeah, well, that's a good way to it. It keeps the instrument moist, see, yeah.
Did you ever wash out your trombone that way too? No,

I'd wash my horn when I'd get through playing. I'd use hot water and soap to wash my horn but as long as I'm playing I go back to play. Then I run it on the end of the system, you know, that's to dampen it up because the horn doesn't sound so good dry. You'll notice that when a fellow picks up a horn and it's dry, he can't get nothing much, but as soon as you pull that water in it and it softens, it seems like it softens the metal or something and you'll get easy tones out of it. And that's what I used to, that's the way I used to play.
